hero.title: Frequently Asked Questions
hero.lead: Start with the questions that matter most on substantial residential projects: project fit, location, scope, budget, permitting, existing conditions, and the path from early review to construction.

intro.title: Plan with fewer unknowns.
intro.text: These answers go deeper than the short FAQ section on the homepage so homeowners can better understand the decisions behind a major renovation.

faqs.question: Is Silver Peak Design Build a registered contractor in Washington?
faqs.answer: Yes. Silver Peak Design & Build’s contractor registration can be verified directly through Washington State Labor & Industries. [View Silver Peak’s official L&I contractor record](https://secure.lni.wa.gov/verify/Detail.aspx?UBI=603006436&LIC=SILVEPC907LT&SAW=).

faqs.question: What types of projects are the best fit for Silver Peak?
faqs.answer: Whole-house renovations, builds and rebuilds, and major additions are our primary focus, followed by ADUs, DADUs, and basement remodels. We also consider kitchens, bathrooms, porches, restoration, and carpentry or tile work when the location, scope, schedule, and budget fit.

faqs.question: What happens during the initial project review?
faqs.answer: First, we review the property's location, project type, goals, scope, budget direction, timing, known conditions, and fit. If it appears aligned, we continue the conversation and decide whether a technical site assessment is the right next step.

faqs.question: When should I schedule a technical site assessment?
faqs.answer: A technical site assessment comes after the initial project-fit review, if Silver Peak determines it is the right next step. It covers existing conditions, access, structure, trees, side sewer, drainage, electrical capacity, and permit needs that could affect design or construction.

faqs.question: Why design-build?
faqs.answer: Design-build brings design and construction planning together from the start. On larger renovations, this helps coordinate structure, utilities, permits, materials, budget, phasing, and construction logistics as one plan.

faqs.question: How do I know whether to renovate, add on, or rebuild?
faqs.answer: It depends on the home's condition, layout, space needs, zoning, and budget. Some homes need reconfiguration or an addition; hidden structural conditions in older homes may make a larger renovation or rebuild more practical.

faqs.question: What should I expect when renovating an older Seattle home?
faqs.answer: Older homes can conceal past work or issues with framing, foundations, plumbing, electrical, drainage, insulation, or water damage. We plan around known conditions, but larger renovations should include contingency for problems found after demolition.

faqs.question: How do permits affect a whole house renovation or addition?
faqs.answer: Permits can affect design and schedule when work changes structure, footprint, living area, plumbing, electrical, stairs, windows, or dwelling use. We identify likely permit and code requirements early so the design can account for them.

faqs.question: How do I build a DADU in Seattle?
faqs.answer: A DADU starts with checking whether the property can support it. Lot layout, access, trees, setbacks, utilities, sewer, drainage, construction staging, goals, and budget all affect feasibility. A project review comes first; if the project appears to fit, a technical site assessment can help determine feasibility.

faqs.question: Should I build an ADU or DADU?
faqs.answer: An ADU is usually within or attached to the home; a DADU is a separate structure. The right option depends on privacy, lot area, access, zoning, utilities, cost, and intended use. Planning an ADU with a whole-house project may coordinate related structural or utility work.

faqs.question: Can a basement remodel become an ADU?
faqs.answer: In many homes, a basement can be evaluated for an ADU, but feasibility depends on ceiling height, safe egress, stairs, moisture, drainage, utilities, heating and ventilation, fire separation, access, and code requirements. Even when an ADU is not the final goal, addressing these conditions during a basement remodel can improve comfort, durability, and long-term flexibility.

faqs.question: What is included in kitchen design and remodeling?
faqs.answer: Kitchen remodeling considers circulation, work zones, appliances, cabinetry, storage, lighting, ventilation, plumbing, and how the room connects to nearby spaces. In a larger renovation, it may also involve structural changes, windows, or the main-floor layout.

faqs.question: What should I plan for in a bathroom remodel?
faqs.answer: Bathroom remodeling should address layout, waterproofing, ventilation, lighting, storage, tile assemblies, fixtures, plumbing locations, accessibility, and durable materials. If the bathroom is part of a larger renovation, it is also worth considering whether walls, door locations, nearby closets, or adjacent rooms should change at the same time.

faqs.question: What bathroom can we use during the remodel?
faqs.answer: If your home has only one bathroom, we may be able to build a temporary bathroom in an unfinished basement or another part of the home. We discuss bathroom access, temporary services, and the construction sequence during planning to help determine whether you can continue living in the home during a major renovation.

faqs.question: Can I live in my home during a major renovation?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, but it depends on the scope. A contained kitchen or bathroom project may allow partial occupancy, while a whole-house renovation, structural rebuild, major addition connection, or extensive utility shutdown may make living in the home impractical. We discuss access, dust control, temporary services, safety, sequencing, and realistic disruption during planning so expectations are clear before construction begins.

faqs.question: How should I think about budget for a major renovation?
faqs.answer: Start with a realistic range rather than a single wish-list number. Larger renovations include design, permitting, site conditions, structural work, utilities, finishes, labor, logistics, and contingency. Sharing a budget direction early helps the team determine whether the scope is aligned and where tradeoffs may be needed before a large amount of design time is spent. [Need help figuring out a realistic budget for your project?](/start-project-review/)

faqs.question: How long does a major renovation take?
faqs.answer: There is no single timeline because permitting, design complexity, structural scope, material lead times, site access, and project size all matter. A whole-house project typically includes a significant preconstruction period before physical work begins. During the project review, we can discuss your target timing and whether it is realistic for the scope you are considering.

faqs.question: How do you handle changes once construction starts?
faqs.answer: Good preconstruction reduces avoidable changes, but larger renovations can still uncover existing conditions or owner decisions that affect the work. When a change is necessary, it should be documented clearly in a change order with the scope, cost, and schedule impact before the work proceeds whenever possible. Clear communication is especially important on projects where one change can affect several trades.

faqs.question: Which areas does Silver Peak serve?
faqs.answer: Silver Peak serves North Seattle and Eastside communities north of I-90. Our primary northern focus includes North Seattle, Bothell, Mill Creek, and Woodinville. We also consider select projects in Redmond and Kirkland when the location, scope, budget, timing, and overall fit make sense. On the Eastside, we prefer projects north of SR 520 when possible. If your project is outside our normal service area and may be a good fit, [fill out our project-review form](/start-project-review/) and we will consider it.

faqs.question: What information should I send when I am ready to start?
faqs.answer: The most helpful starting information is the project address, the type of work you are considering, what is not working today, what you want the home to become, your approximate budget range, ideal timing, and any plans, photos, reports, or known property issues you already have. You do not need every answer. The purpose of the project review is to organize the important first questions and determine the best next step.

cta.title: Have a project that needs a closer look?
cta.text: Share the location, scope, budget direction, and what you want to build. We will review the fit before recommending the next step.
